To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
general practitioners' perceptions, beliefs, and attitudes about patients with irritable bowl syndrome and chronic fatigue are important determinants of the care provided to these patients.
general practitioners' perceptions and beliefs about chronic fatigue syndrome and its management differ from those for irritable bowel syndrome.

general practitioners tend to stereotype patients with CFS as having certain undesirable qualities, and this is due to a lack of a precise physical location of the condition; its reclassification over time; transgressing of social roles; and conflicts between doctors and patients over causes and management.
In summary, our research is concerned with

general practitioners' beliefs about chronic fatigue syndrome, their perceptions of the syndrome compared with irritable bowl syndrome, and the implications of their beliefs and perceptions for treatment.

the way in which the beliefs that general practitioners hold about patients with two common syndromes, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), may affect the way in which they treat them.
the way in which the general practitioner's perception of a patient's condition affects his or her management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the management of patients with chronic and irritable bowel and syndrome is suboptimal because of doctors' beliefs, and this is a problem in the NHS.
the management of these syndromes is often suboptimal.

the general practitioners were not aware that they did not know how to manage these patients and that they were not able to access any information that would enable them to manage the patients effectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a need for a more systematic approach to the education of general practitioners about chronic fatigue syndrome.
we found a number of factors that could contribute to the negative stereotyping of CFS patients and that this in turn could contribute to the difficulties in the clinical management of patients.
the doctors' beliefs about chronic fatigue syndrome and their beliefs about the best management strategies for the condition are not consistent with the evidence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way that patients with chronic fatigue and irritable bowel are perceived by doctors has a profound impact on how they are treated.
there is a lack of evidence based treatment options for patients with chronic fatigue.

doctors need to be aware of the social and psychological factors that may influence the way patients with irritable bowl syndrome or chronic fatigue syndrome present to their doctor and to be able to manage these factors in a positive way.
